---
title: "A1 self-check — Organisation and regulation"
---

Answer before opening each explanation. If an answer is uncertain, return
to the [tutorial](index.qmd) and redraw the relevant mechanism.

## 1. Is glucose in the gut lumen already absorbed?

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Answer

No. Absorption requires crossing the absorptive epithelium into an internal
route. The lumen is continuous with the exterior; digestion and absorption
are different processes.
:::

## 2. Double a cube's side: what happens to its area-to-volume ratio?

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Answer

Area increases fourfold and volume eightfold, so the ratio halves. Since
$A/V=6/L$, its units are inverse length. A real animal can increase functional
area with folds or branching and use bulk flow over long distances.
:::

## 3. Does one layer of flat cells prove that a section is a lung?

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Answer

No. It supports a thin epithelial arrangement compatible with exchange, but
many locations contain thin epithelia. Organ identification needs surrounding
architecture, scale and other features. Observe first; support the inference.
:::

## 4. Is a helpful response positive feedback?

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Answer

Not necessarily. Feedback sign describes whether the consequence opposes or
amplifies the initial change. A response that reduces a temperature rise is
negative feedback even if it is beneficial.
:::

## 5. Does a stable internal concentration mean no transport is occurring?

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Answer

No. Inputs and outputs can balance while substantial transport and energy use
continue. Homeostasis is dynamic maintenance, not universal inactivity.
:::

## 6. Has a fish evolved if its physiology changes after weeks in warmer water?

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Answer

That observation describes adjustment within an individual, compatible with
acclimation. Demonstrating evolutionary adaptation requires evidence about
heritable features and population change across generations, not just one
individual's useful response.
:::
